prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Time, Once, October

outputs.L1:
Time collapses between the lips of strangers. My days collapse into a hollow tube, then implode against the present like an iron wall. My eyes are blocked with rubble, a smear of perspectives blurring every horizon. In the breathless precision of silence, one word is made.

Once the renegade flesh was gone, the autumn air lay against my face, sharp and blue as a needle. But rain fell throughout October, and death lay as a condemnation within my blood.

The smell of your neck in August—a fine gold wire bejeweling war. All the rest lies illusive, like a farmhouse on the other side of a valley, vanishing in the afternoon.

Day three, day four, day ten; the seventh step, a veiled door leading to my golden anniversary—flameproofed, free-paper shredded in the teeth of a pillaging dog, never to dream of spiders. And when they turned the hoses upon me: a burst of light.
outputs.L2:
Between unfamiliar mouths, time folds in on itself, and my days narrow into an empty cylinder that will soon strike the present and crumple against its iron barrier. Debris seals my vision; viewpoints run together, smudging every skyline. Within silence’s airless exactness, a single word takes shape.

After the rebellious body had disappeared, autumn air touched my face, blue and piercing like a needle. Yet rain continued throughout October, while death remained in my blood like a sentence passed against me.

In August, the scent of your neck was a slender golden thread adorning the machinery of war. Everything else stays indistinct, like a farmhouse across the valley fading from sight as afternoon advances.

The third day, the fourth, the tenth; the seventh stair; a curtained entrance opening onto my golden anniversary—made fire-resistant, reduced to scraps of free paper between the jaws of a marauding dog. I would never again dream about spiders. And when they aimed the hoses at me, light erupted.
outputs.L3:
Time and perception gradually collapse into confusion, leaving the speaker unable to distinguish past from present or memory from immediate experience. Emotional pain accumulates alongside vivid sensory fragments, forming a kind of debris that obscures the world and traps the speaker within grief.

After the loss of the body, autumn introduces a painful clarity. Its cold air, fading light, and natural decay sharpen the speaker’s awareness of mortality. The season becomes more than a setting: it embodies the inescapable knowledge that death has entered the speaker’s life and permanently altered how reality is perceived.

Yet the remembered presence of a loved one still offers a fragile form of beauty. Fleeting traces of intimacy survive amid images of violence, separation, and disappearance. Although memory cannot restore what has been lost, it briefly resists destruction by preserving a sense of connection across physical and emotional distance.

As the days pass, the speaker moves through a series of symbolic thresholds. These transitions suggest a journey, but one that is fragmented rather than continuous or purposeful. Each boundary crossed appears to bring the speaker closer to an uncertain milestone—perhaps acceptance, understanding, or transformation—without guaranteeing that it can ever be fully reached.

Ultimately, the accumulated images of destruction and suffering culminate in a sudden burst of light. This illumination does not erase the grief that precedes it, but it hints at revelation or transcendence. In the final moment, devastation gives way to the possibility that pain may produce insight, and that even amid death and disappearance, some form of meaning may still emerge.
outputs.L4:
The poem meditates on time, mortality, memory, and physical suffering through a structure that resists straightforward narration. Rather than unfolding chronologically, it moves between moments, images, and sensations, reproducing the unstable movement of memory itself. Past and present seem to overlap, suggesting that painful experiences are never entirely left behind but continue to shape the speaker’s consciousness.

Surreal imagery and shifting sensory impressions intensify this atmosphere of uncertainty. Images may appear vivid without being fully explained, while sounds, colors, textures, and bodily sensations blur into one another. This fragmentation reflects both the vulnerability of the body and the difficulty of giving coherent form to experiences of loss or violence. The body becomes a place where time is registered: suffering leaves traces, and mortality is felt not as an abstract idea but as an immediate physical reality.

Yet the poem does not remain entirely within despair. Even amid devastation, it discovers brief moments of beauty, clarity, and illumination. These moments do not erase suffering, but they interrupt it, offering a temporary sense of connection or understanding. Memory therefore becomes more than a record of what has been lost. By reshaping experience through language and imagination, it can transform pain into something that carries significance.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that meaning is fragile but still possible. Time destroys, bodies suffer, and memories fragment, yet the act of remembering allows moments of beauty to survive. Through its broken chronology and intense imagery, the poem shows how art can hold violence and illumination together, turning even devastation into a fleeting but meaningful form of transcendence.
outputs.L5:
### Once in October

Once, in October, Time seemed to pause.

The clocks still moved, of course, but the afternoon lingered beneath amber trees, and every falling leaf appeared to choose its path carefully. We walked without speaking, listening to the soft rhythm of our footsteps and the distant bells from the town.

We believed the moment would last forever.

Years later, I returned to that same road. The trees were taller, the bells sounded quieter, and you were only a memory. Yet when the wind lifted the leaves, October opened its golden door again—and for one brief moment, Time gave me back what it had taken.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist prose poem about time, memory, illness, lost intimacy, and violence, using fragmented syntax and vivid sensory imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
At three in the morning the clocks begin molting.

Their little silver skins drift through the hospital corridor, catching on the IV poles, the blue wrists, the mouths half-open under sleep. Somewhere a machine keeps saying *still, still, still* in a green voice.

You lie beneath the sheets like a country after snow.

I remember your shoulder—no, the lamp beside it—no, the rain chewing the window while we forgot our names. Intimacy was a warm animal then. It drank from our hands. It slept between our ribs.

Now memory arrives wearing rubber gloves.

It touches nothing.

In the cup: two pills, pale as knocked-out teeth. In the wall: pipes full of winter. Beneath your tongue: the metallic dusk of blood, of coins, of all the words bitten through before they could become mercy.

Time enters with a hammer.

Not loudly. Not at first.

A crack in the mirror. A bruise ripening under the calendar. Tuesday dragged behind the house by its hair. The years kneeling in the kitchen among broken plates, asking which of us struck first.

I say: the door.

You say: the war.

But the war was only a red bird trapped in the room, beating itself against every surface—glass, bone, photograph—until even love wore feathers of damage.

Once, your hand knew the dark geography of my back. Once, I could find you by breath alone.

Now your fingers hover over mine, five pale questions.

Outside, ambulances stitch and unstitch the night. Snow falls upward. The moon smells of antiseptic and burned wool. In the next bed, an old woman calls for a child who has been dead sixty years, and the child answers through the radiator:

*I am coming.*

*I am almost born.*

Morning gathers at the window, yellow and surgical.

The clocks crawl back into their wounds.

You close your eyes. Or open them somewhere I cannot follow.

Between us, the warm animal lifts its ruined head.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental stream-of-consciousness paragraph in the style of mid-century confessional poetry, with no line breaks and an ominous, dreamlike tone.
counterfactuals.output: At three in the morning the mirror began to breathe, and I, faithless daughter of a house gone dark, counted each silver inhalation as if it were a debt; somewhere beneath the floorboards my childhood dragged its small red wagon from room to room, carrying the teeth I had lost, the prayers I had swallowed, the names of men I mistook for doors, and I wanted to call out but my mouth was full of black feathers, my hands were two pale witnesses refusing the oath, while the moon leaned close as a nurse with a needle and whispered that morning was only another rumor, that the garden had already buried its knives, that the bed beside me was not empty but waiting, waiting with the patience of snow, and then the clock struck no hour at all, yet every locked thing in the house opened its eyes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense prose poem that moves through autumn, mortality, war, anniversaries, and repression, including images of rubble, rain, a lover’s neck, a farmhouse, spiders, and fire hoses.
counterfactuals.output: Autumn enters wearing the smoke of ruined houses, its pockets full of acorns and shrapnel, and every anniversary rings from the calendar like a spoon struck against a prison pipe. In the square, rain varnishes the rubble; soldiers pass beneath torn flags while old women count the dead by the names they no longer say aloud. I remember the farmhouse at dusk, its red boards darkening toward blood, spiders stitching the rafters to the cold, your neck bent over the basin—pale, mortal, briefly mine—as if tenderness were a country no map had betrayed. We believed the harvest might forgive us, though the fields had learned the weight of boots, though letters arrived with their sentences blacked out, though windows listened. Now fire hoses uncoil through the streets like blind blue veins, beating students from the statues, washing chalk, petitions, and birthdays into the drains. Each year returns with the same wet hands: the armistice, the disappearance, the wedding, the first frost. Leaves flare and fall against the barricades. Under them, the earth keeps all its censored testimony—bone, button, bullet, seed—while rain speaks without permission, and in the abandoned farmhouse one small spider crosses the cracked photograph, patient as history, delicate as the pulse beneath your neck.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an abstract literary monologue narrated by someone whose memories are collapsing, blending romantic nostalgia with bodily dread and political violence.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember you best in fragments the state has not yet confiscated.

Your wrist turning beneath the café table. Rain making small republics in the street. The blue dress—or was it green?—with one loose thread at the shoulder, which I wanted to pull with my teeth until the whole summer came undone.

There had been music. I know this because my body leans toward an absent sound.

But the rooms are failing now. Doors open onto other doors; childhood enters wearing the face of tomorrow. My mother stands at the sink washing blood from a plate, though perhaps it was only beetroot, perhaps it was not my mother. Every object has begun rehearsing its alibi.

The doctor says memory is electrical. A weather passing through meat.

I dislike the word meat.

At night, my left hand no longer believes in me. It lies beside my hip like a captured animal, warm but unconvinced. My heart knocks from inside its little prison, asking who signed the order. I tell it: Be quiet. They are listening. The ribs, those pale officials, keep their files in darkness.

Do you remember the checkpoint by the river?

No—do not answer. If you answer incorrectly, you will vanish.

The soldiers were very young. That is what made them terrible. Their faces still had the soft unfinished look of boys interrupted while dreaming. One held our papers upside down. Another stroked the barrel of his rifle as if soothing a horse. Behind them, the city burned without flame: windows sealed, statues hooded, names scraped from walls. Even the pigeons seemed to have been issued instructions.

You squeezed my hand once.

Or I squeezed yours.

Or there was no hand, only the idea of tenderness crossing a border illegally.

We had promised to leave before the speeches hardened into laws. We had promised many things in those days because promises were the only currency not yet devalued. We would go south. We would live near the sea. You would grow basil on the sill; I would translate poems no one wanted. Each morning, salt would gather on our skin, and history would lose our address.

Instead, history came upstairs.

Boots in the stairwell. A fist against wood. The black mouth of the van.

Afterward, I kept finding your hair everywhere: on the pillow, in my coat, curled around the soap like a question too intimate for language. Years passed. Governments changed their uniforms. The dead were renumbered. Your photograph faded first at the eyes.

Now the face in it could belong to anyone I have loved, which is to say anyone I have failed to save.

There are mornings when my teeth taste of iron and all the mirrors are crowded with strangers. One of them mouths my name. I cannot hear him through the glass. I place my palm against his palm and feel nothing but cold—the cold of hospital corridors, interrogation rooms, winter monuments.

Still, somewhere, it is June.

You are laughing because I have spilled wine on the blanket. The grass presses its green alphabet into your knees. Far off, a siren begins, but we mistake it for singing. We are innocent of the future. We kiss with the arrogance of people who believe the body is a country no army can enter.

Forgive us.

They entered.

They entered with decrees and needles, with census lists and rubber stamps. They entered through the mouth, the ear, the soft machinery of sleep. They changed the street names first, then the names of the missing, then the meaning of missing. They taught us to say relocated, processed, unfortunate. They made language wear gloves.

And now language is leaving me too.

Words fall away while I am speaking. I reach for rose and find wound. I reach for morning and find siren. I reach for your name—

Your name—

It was something warm. Something with a door in it.

Listen: if I forget you entirely, it will not mean they have won. Forgetting is not surrender. It is only the last room collapsing after the house has burned. Beneath it, under ash and plaster, the earth keeps the shape of every foundation.

Come closer, whoever you are.

Let me borrow your face.

Tell me we stood by the river. Tell me the soldiers lowered their guns. Tell me we crossed safely and lived among white curtains swollen with sea wind. Tell me my hands were gentle. Tell me my body was once more than this frightened province, this trembling archive, this border closing in the dark.

Lie to me beautifully.

There is so little time, and I would like to remember the lie.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write one long, punctuation-light surreal poem in which time becomes physical, perspectives blur, October rain carries death, and the final image is a burst of light.
counterfactuals.output:
time climbed out of the clocks at dawn  
dragging its long blue body through the kitchen  
and every chair grew older beneath it  

I touched an hour on the floor  
it was warm as bread  
it trembled in my palm  
then opened one black eye  

outside the houses leaned into October  
their windows full of sleeping water  
their chimneys remembering forests  
that had never existed  

rain came down carrying death  
not loudly  
not with thunder or ruined wings  
but softly in each silver thread  
a small cold animal  
a name erased from stone  
the last breath of apples sinking into grass  

I walked beneath it  
or someone wearing my distance walked  
while I remained behind the glass  
watching my own shoulders vanish  
into the wet arithmetic of streets  

the sky looked up at me from every puddle  
and I looked down from the sky  
my face divided among gutters  
my hands drifting over rooftops  
my footsteps falling from clouds  

time gathered around my ankles  
thick as river clay  
years clung to my shoes  
minutes nested in my sleeves  
a century slept under my tongue  
and when I spoke  
the dead turned gently in the rain  

they were not ghosts  
they were doors without houses  
lamps without rooms  
the pale interiors of bells  
swinging beneath the earth  

one of them held my childhood  
like a cup filled to the rim  
one wore the future as a veil  
one had my eyes  
though I was using them elsewhere  

we crossed each other without meeting  
we exchanged shadows  
we borrowed mouths  
we dreamed from opposite ends of the same skull  

October deepened  
its red leaves entering the ground  
like letters no one would answer  
its crows sewing darkness  
from field to field  

the rain kept falling  
and every drop contained a small departure  
a bed cooling in an empty room  
a coat left breathing on a nail  
a photograph learning to forget  
a pulse traveling farther than the body  

I felt the road become my spine  
the river enter my veins  
the hills lift slowly behind my eyes  
until near and far were broken mirrors  
and I could no longer tell  
whether I carried the world  
or the world carried me  

then time rose upright before us  
enormous and tender  
its ribs made of calendars  
its blood bright with unfinished hours  
it reached into its chest  
and drew out the first morning  

the dead opened their rain filled hands  
the clocks released their birds  
the earth turned inside out  
and from the wound of the horizon came  

a burst of light
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
